\chapter{Cycle Space Bond Space}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Cycle Space Bond Space}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.CycleSpaceBondSpace.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[B&M's unimodular (Thm 12.3, p. 226): every \emph{full} square submatrix (order $\nu- 1$, selected by an\dots]
\lean{Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\label{Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\leanok
"Full" means as large as the matrix allows --- for a $(\nu-1) \times \varepsilon$ basis
matrix of the bond space, the square submatrices of order $\nu - 1$.  Theorem 12.3
says such a basis matrix is unimodular, and that is exactly what makes theorem
12.4's determinant count the spanning trees: each nonsingular full submatrix
contributes $(\pm 1)^{2} = 1$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} \texttt{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular}, which quantifies over
\emph{all} square submatrices --- that is B&M's strictly stronger \emph{totally} unimodular of
exercise 12.2.3, stated separately below.  "Full square submatrix" is rendered as
\texttt{M.submatrix id g} for an injective $g : n \to m$: all rows, and \texttt{card n} columns
chosen injectively.  Placed in the \texttt{Matrix} namespace so it reads
\texttt{B.IsUnimodular}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[B&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222)]
\lean{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
\label{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
\leanok
Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the
vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix, distinct from the $0/1$ matrix of \S{}1.3, and they encode
the conservation condition exactly: $M *_{v} f = 0$ says inflow balances outflow at
every vertex.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib: \texttt{SimpleGraph.incMatrix} is the
\emph{unoriented} $0/1$ matrix, and the oriented version is one of Mathlib's own open
TODOs.  B&M's "if $a$ is a link" clause (i.e. loops map to $0$) is \textbf{automatic} in
this encoding: a loop has \texttt{tail a = head a = v}, so the two indicators cancel to
$1 - 1 = 0$.  Stated over a general \texttt{[Ring R]} so the same definition serves the
$F$-valued \S{}12.1 and the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued \S{}12.2.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The cycle space $\mathcal{C}$: circulations, i.e]
\lean{CycleSpace.cycleSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.cycleSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
Currents that flow round and round without accumulating anywhere.
\textbf{!} Contrast chapter 11, where conservation was imposed only at \emph{intermediate}
vertices; here it holds \textbf{everywhere}, so there is no net source or sink.

The conservation condition (12.1) is packaged as
$M *_{v} f = 0$, i.e. \texttt{f $\in$ ker M.mulVecLin} --- theorem 12.1's second half is precisely
the claim that this repackaging is faithful.  Defining $\mathcal{C}$ as a \texttt{Submodule}
directly gives the vector-space structure the book verifies by hand.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The bond space $\mathcal{B}$: potential differences, i.e]
\lean{CycleSpace.bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.bondSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
Assign a voltage to every vertex and read off the drop across every
wire.  Theorem 12.1 identifies $\mathcal{B}$ as the row space of $M$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as its
orthogonal complement --- the duality organising the whole chapter.

$\delta p$ is $M^{T} \emph{_{v} p$, so $\mathcal{B}$ is the }range* of that map.  \textbf{!} Note
the asymmetry with \texttt{cycleSpace}: $\mathcal{C}$ is a \textbf{kernel} and $\mathcal{B}$ a \textbf{range}, which is
why theorem 12.2(ii) is a genuinely separate argument rather than a formal dual of
(i).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The standard dot-product bilinear form on $K \to K$ (here $A \to F$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.dotForm}
\label{CycleSpace.dotForm}
\leanok
$f$ and $g$ are orthogonal when $\sum_{a \in A} f(a)g(a) = 0$.  For real
coefficients this is the usual inner product; but the chapter also needs it over
fields of characteristic $p$ (exercise 12.2.4), where the form is \textbf{degenerate} and
a vector can be orthogonal to itself.  That degeneracy is precisely why Shank's
result --- \texttt{dim($\mathcal{B}$\_F $\cap$ $\mathcal{C}$\_F) > 0} iff $p \mid \tau(G)$ --- is possible at all: over $\mathbb{R}$ the two
spaces meet only in zero.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} an inner product, and deliberately so.  Used with
\texttt{LinearMap.BilinForm.orthogonal}, which works over every field --- in particular
\texttt{ZMod p} --- unlike \texttt{Submodule.orthogonal}/$^{\perp}$, which needs \texttt{RCLike} and would make
exercise 12.2.4 unstateable.  The four $mk_{2}$ obligations are bilinearity, all
discharged by \texttt{simp} on sums.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$G$ is the underlying (simple) graph of the digraph \texttt{(tail, head)}]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
\label{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
\leanok
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when some arc runs between them
in one direction or the other.  The chapter's counting results --- \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = $\nu$ - $\omega$},
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$}, $\tau(G)$ --- are all statements about this underlying graph, the
orientation being an auxiliary device that cancels out.

\textbf{!} A \texttt{SimpleGraph} underlying graph loses information the arc
carrier has: loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs both vanish.  That is
harmless for the \emph{counting} results, which are about $G$, but means $G$ does not
determine \texttt{(tail, head)} --- hence this is a relation, not a function.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{(tail, head)} is an orientation of the simple graph $G$]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf}
\label{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
$G$ is recovered by forgetting directions.  The point of \S{}12.2 is that
$\tau(G)$ is an invariant of $G$ alone, yet is most easily computed through the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix of an arbitrarily chosen orientation --- the signs cancel
in the determinant, which is exactly what exercise 12.2.2(a) makes precise.

\textbf{!} Definitionally equal to \texttt{IsUnderlyingGraph}, so "orientation
of $G$" here means only "has $G$ as underlying graph" --- it does \textbf{not} forbid $D$
from having both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$, which chapter 10's \texttt{IsOrientationOf} does.
For this chapter that is deliberate and harmless: the results are about $M$ and
\texttt{MM$^{T}$}, which tolerate digons and loops.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[An arc-level cycle in the digraph, as a nonempty closed arc-sequence]
\lean{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
\label{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
A cycle of the \emph{underlying} graph, traversed in one of its two
directions; some arcs point along the direction of travel and some against it,
which is what the sign in $f_C$ records.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this structure is degenerate.}  It carries only a nonempty list of
arcs, with \textbf{no} closed-walk condition and \textbf{no} distinctness condition --- the
docstring's "the closed/interior-distinct invariants are elided" understates the
cost.  As a result \emph{any} nonempty list of arcs is an \texttt{ArcCycle}, and the derived
predicate collapses:

    IsArcAcyclic tail head S  $\leftrightarrow$  S = $\emptyset$

(for nonempty $S$, pick $a \in S$ and take the one-element list $[a]$).  Downstream,
theorem 12.2(i) then reads \emph{"the columns of $B | S$ are independent iff $S = \emptyset$"} ---
false --- and lemma 12.2.1 becomes trivially true for the wrong reason.  This is not
\texttt{sorry}, which makes it more dangerous: the definition \emph{looks} honest.

\emph{The repair} needs three fields beyond \texttt{arcs} and \texttt{nonempty}:
\item \textbf{closed walk} --- a vertex sequence \texttt{verts : List V} with \texttt{verts.length = arcs.length}
  such that consecutive arcs meet head-to-tail, cyclically: for each $i$,
  \texttt{\{tail arcs[i], head arcs[i]\} = \{verts[i], verts[i+1 mod n]\}} (the set form allows
  an arc to be traversed against its direction, which is exactly what $C^{+}$ records);
\item \textbf{interior distinctness} --- \texttt{verts.Nodup};
\item optionally \textbf{no repeated arc} --- \texttt{arcs.Nodup}.

\textbf{!} \texttt{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle} genuinely cannot serve, as the note says: the chapter's
digraphs admit loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs, which a \texttt{SimpleGraph}
cannot express.  But that argues for building the structure properly, not for
omitting its invariants.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$S \subseteq A$ is acyclic: it contains no arc-cycle]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsArcAcyclic}
\label{CycleSpace.IsArcAcyclic}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
No cycle of the digraph lies entirely inside $S$.  Theorem 12.2 makes
this combinatorial property equivalent to a linear-algebraic one --- the bridge that
turns counting spanning trees into counting nonsingular submatrices.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective by inheritance.}  Because \texttt{ArcCycle} has no closure or distinctness
conditions, this predicate collapses to $S = \emptyset$; see \texttt{ArcCycle}'s docstring for the
one-line argument and the repair.  The definition here is *correct given a correct
\texttt{ArcCycle}* --- nothing needs changing at this declaration.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$f_C$: the circulation of an oriented cycle ($\pm 1$ on $C^{+} / C^{-}$, $0$ off $C$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.cycleCirculation}
\label{CycleSpace.cycleCirculation}
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
Send one unit of current round the cycle in the chosen direction; arcs
pointing with the flow carry $+1$, those against it $-1$, everything else nothing.
Conservation holds at every vertex because the cycle enters and leaves each of its
vertices exactly once.  These are the elementary circulations from which all others
are built, and they give the cycle space its name.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  $f_C$ is an opaque function, so
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest} --- whose rows are these --- asserts nothing.

\emph{The repair} depends on repairing \texttt{ArcCycle} first: once a cycle carries its vertex
sequence, $C^{+}$ is definable (arc $i$ is in $C^{+}$ when \texttt{tail arcs[i] = verts[i]}, i.e.
it is traversed forwards), and

    f_C a = if a $\notin$ arcs then 0 else if a $\in$ C$^{+}$ then 1 else -1

\textbf{!} With \texttt{arcs} a \texttt{List}, $a \in C^{+}$ needs the \emph{position}, not just membership --- an arc
could in principle occur twice.  Adding \texttt{arcs.Nodup} to \texttt{ArcCycle} removes that
ambiguity and is the cleaner route.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[B&M's edge cut $(S, \bar{S})$: the arcs with exactly one end in $S$]
\lean{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
\label{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
\leanok
The arcs crossing the boundary of $S$, in either direction.  The
\emph{direction} matters for the associated potential difference $g_B$, which takes $+1$
on arcs leaving $S$ and $-1$ on those entering it --- the edge cut is undirected, its
potential difference is not.

A \texttt{Set A}, not a \texttt{Finset}, matching \texttt{IsBond}'s quantification
over arbitrary \texttt{S : Set V}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A bond: a MINIMAL nonempty edge cut. \textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBond}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBond}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
An edge cut with nothing to spare.  Bonds are dual to cycles: lemma
12.2.2 says the support of a nonzero potential difference contains a bond, exactly
as lemma 12.2.1 says the support of a nonzero circulation contains a cycle.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib --- and beware two false friends.
\texttt{Dart.lean} uses "bond" for an unrelated half-edge notion, and the repo's
\texttt{IsEdgeCut} is a \emph{cut} without the minimality clause, on a different carrier.

\textbf{!} The minimality clause here quantifies over subsets $B' \subseteq B$ that are \textbf{themselves
edge cuts} (\texttt{$\exists$ S', B' = edgeCutSet S'}).  That is the right reading of "minimal
nonempty edge cut" and is stronger than minimality among arbitrary subsets; check it
against use sites, since lemma 12.2.2 only produces an edge cut inside the support
and then needs a \emph{bond} inside that.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$g_B$: the potential difference of a bond, $p =$ indicator of $S$ (B&M give it, p. 221)]
\lean{CycleSpace.bondPotentialDiff}
\label{CycleSpace.bondPotentialDiff}
\leanok
Put every vertex of $S$ at voltage $1$ and every other at $0$; the
drops are $+1$ on arcs leaving $S$, $-1$ on arcs entering, $0$ on arcs with both
ends on one side.  These are the elementary potential differences, and they give the
bond space its name.

Defined directly by the book's $\delta p$ formula with $p$ the
indicator of $S$, rather than by the three-case rule --- that makes membership in $\mathcal{B}$
immediate and turns the book's "it can be verified" into \texttt{rfl}.  Note the definition
takes an arbitrary \texttt{S : Set V}, not a bond, so $g_B$ exists for any vertex set; the
bond condition matters only for the \emph{basis} claims.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A basis matrix of a submodule $W \le (A \to F)$: its rows are a basis of $W$]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix}
\leanok
Package a basis as the rows of a matrix, so questions about the space
become questions about the matrix.  This is what lets theorem 12.2 phrase acyclicity
as linear independence of \emph{columns}, and theorem 12.4 count spanning trees by a
determinant.

"Rows form a basis" is unfolded into its two halves ---
\texttt{LinearIndependent F M} and \texttt{span (range M) = W} --- rather than using \texttt{Basis}, which
would require a chosen index equivalence.  The row index $n$ is a free \texttt{Fintype},
so the same predicate serves matrices indexed by $T$, by $T^{c}$, or by ${v // v \ne y}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Restrict Cols]
\lean{CycleSpace.restrictCols}
\label{CycleSpace.restrictCols}
\leanok
$M | S$ --- B&M's column restriction (\texttt{Matrix.submatrix}).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A spanning tree of the digraph]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree}
\label{CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree}
A maximal acyclic set of arcs touching every vertex.  By theorem 12.2,
spanning trees are exactly the $(\nu-1)$-element subsets $S$ for which $B | S$ is
nonsingular --- which is what makes \S{}12.2's determinant formula count them.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body --- the most damaging one in the file.}  \texttt{tau} counts the
\texttt{Finset}s satisfying this predicate, so \textbf{$\tau(G)$ is an opaque natural number}, and
every \S{}12.2 statement about it is vacuous: theorem 12.4, (12.8), corollary 12.4, the
matrix-tree theorem, and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.2(b), 12.2.4(a), (b).

\emph{The repair}, once \texttt{ArcCycle} is fixed:

    IsSpanningTree tail head T := IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ T.card + 1 = Fintype.card V
                                  $\land$ (the underlying subgraph on T is connected)

or equivalently "acyclic and spanning", using the connectivity notion suggested for
\texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}.  Acyclic plus $|T| = \nu - 1$ already forces connectivity for a
graph on $\nu$ vertices, so the middle clause plus acyclicity suffices --- but only once
\texttt{IsArcAcyclic} is genuine.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A maximal forest of the digraph]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
\label{CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
A maximal acyclic set of arcs --- a spanning tree of each component.
Its size $\nu - \omega$ is exactly the rank of the bond space, which is how corollary 12.2
computes \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$}.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  Makes both tree-basis theorems
(\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest},
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}) vacuous, and is a hypothesis of
\texttt{fundamentalCycle}.

\emph{The repair:} \texttt{IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ $\forall$ a $\notin$ T, $\lnot$ IsArcAcyclic tail head (insert a T)}
--- acyclic and maximally so.  Note this is the \emph{forest} notion, weaker than
\texttt{IsSpanningTree}: it does not require connectivity, which is exactly why corollary
12.2 gets $\nu - \omega$ rather than $\nu - 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The fundamental cycle of $a \notin T$ ($T + a$ contains a unique cycle)]
\lean{CycleSpace.fundamentalCycle}
\label{CycleSpace.fundamentalCycle}
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle, CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
The tree already provides a unique route between the ends of $a$
(theorem 2.1), and adding $a$ closes exactly one cycle.  The $\varepsilon - \nu + \omega$ fundamental
cycles, one per non-tree arc, give the tree-basis of the cycle space --- the matrix
$C$ is a basis matrix because $C | \bar{T}$ is an identity matrix, so its rank is full.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  An opaque \texttt{ArcCycle}, so
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest} asserts nothing about it.

\emph{The repair.}  The lever noted in the source comment is right: \texttt{IsAcyclic.path\_unique}
gives the unique $T$-path between $a$'s ends, and the cycle is that path closed by
$a$.  \textbf{!} But it is stated for \texttt{SimpleGraph}, while this chapter's carrier is
\texttt{tail, head : A $\to$ V} with loops and parallel arcs --- so either transfer along the
underlying graph (losing the multi-arc case) or redo the uniqueness argument on the
arc carrier.  The \texttt{hT} hypothesis is what makes "unique" true, and $ha : a \notin T$ what
makes the cycle exist.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The vertex set $S$ of the fundamental bond of $a \in T$ ($\bar{T} + a$ contains a unique bond, B&M's\dots]
\lean{CycleSpace.fundamentalBondVertexSet}
\label{CycleSpace.fundamentalBondVertexSet}
Deleting $a$ splits its tree in two, and $S$ is the vertex set of one
half; the arcs crossing between the halves form the fundamental bond.  The $\nu - \omega$
fundamental bonds, one per tree arc, give the tree-basis of the bond space, with
$B | T$ an identity matrix.  The exact mirror of the fundamental cycle --- theorem 2.6
is to bonds and cotrees as theorem 2.5 is to cycles and spanning trees.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  Makes \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}
vacuous.

\emph{The repair:} $S$ is the set of vertices reachable from \texttt{tail a} in $T \ {a}$ (using
the underlying-graph reachability of \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}'s repair).  Then
\texttt{edgeCutSet tail head S} is the fundamental bond, and \texttt{bondPotentialDiff tail head S}
its potential difference --- which is why the definition returns the \emph{vertex set}
rather than the bond, letting \texttt{bondPotentialDiff} be applied directly.
\textbf{!} Leans on B&M's theorem 2.6, which is out of chapter and not in this repo.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the bond space (rows indexed by $T$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree}
Its defining feature is that $B | T$ is an identity matrix --- the
fundamental bond of $a$ contains $a$ itself with coefficient $1$ and no other tree
arc.  That is what pins down \texttt{det(B | T) = 1} in the proof of theorem 12.3, and
what makes exercise 12.1.2(b)'s change-of-basis identity readable.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  This predicate is a hypothesis of theorems 12.3,
12.4, corollary 12.4 and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.3(a), 12.2.4(a) --- all of which
therefore constrain nothing.

\emph{The repair:} $B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix when its rows are the fundamental-bond
potential differences, i.e.

    B = fun a : {a // a $\in$ T} => bondPotentialDiff tail head (fundamentalBondVertexSet tail head T a.1)

--- exactly the matrix appearing in \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}.  \textbf{!}
Alternatively, characterise it axiomatically as *"a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$ whose
restriction $B | T$ is the identity"*, which is weaker to state, enough for theorem
12.3, and does not depend on \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} --- probably the better
choice, since it is the property every proof actually uses.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$C$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the cycle space (rows indexed by $\bar{T}$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree'}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree'}
The cycle-side mirror of \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree}: $C | \bar{T}$ is the
identity, because the fundamental cycle of $a$ is the only one using $a$.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  Hypothesis of (12.8), corollary 12.4 and exercises
12.2.1(b), 12.2.4(a) --- all vacuous as a result.

\emph{The repair:} as for \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree}, either concretely (rows are the
fundamental-cycle circulations) or axiomatically (*a basis matrix of $\mathcal{C}$ with
$C | \bar{T}$ the identity*).  The axiomatic form is again preferable and is what the
determinant arguments actually consume.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\tau(G)$: the number of spanning trees]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau}
\label{CycleSpace.tau}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree}
The object \S{}12.2 exists to compute.  Theorem 2.8 gave a recursion and
theorem 2.9 a closed formula for complete graphs; chapter 12 finally delivers the
general determinant formula --- the \textbf{matrix-tree theorem}, implicit in Kirchhoff
(1847).

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective by inheritance.}  \texttt{IsSpanningTree} has a \texttt{sorry} body, so \texttt{tau} counts
an opaque predicate and is itself opaque.  \textbf{This is the single most consequential
defect in the file} --- every \S{}12.2 result is a statement about \texttt{tau}.  Nothing here
needs changing; repairing \texttt{IsSpanningTree} repairs this.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[bondSpace_eq_rowSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.bondSpace_eq_rowSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.bondSpace_eq_rowSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
, first half.  *Let $M$ be the incidence matrix of a digraph
$D$.  Then $\mathcal{B}$ is the row space of $M$.*

The drop across $a$ is the signed combination of the vertex potentials,
with $m_v$ picking out the sign.  So the bond space is \emph{exactly} the row space of
$M$, and \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = rank M}.

\texttt{Submodule.span F (Set.range M)} is the row space, $M$ being read
as a family of rows indexed by $V$.  Step 3's identity is the only real content and
is worth extracting, since theorem 12.1's second half needs it too.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[cycleSpace_eq_orthogonal_bondSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.cycleSpace_eq_orthogonal_bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.cycleSpace_eq_orthogonal_bondSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.cycleSpace, CycleSpace.dotForm}
, second half.  \emph{\dotsand $\mathcal{C}$ is its orthogonal complement.}

This duality is the organising idea of the chapter.  It gives corollary
12.2's dimension formula at once, it makes \texttt{BC' = 0} in corollary 12.4, and it is the
source of the cycle/bond symmetry that, as B&M remark, *finds its proper setting in
the theory of matroids*.

\textbf{!} Note this is orthogonality for a possibly \textbf{degenerate} form ---
over \texttt{ZMod p} a space need not be complementary to its orthogonal, which is exactly
what exercise 12.2.4(b) exploits.  So "orthogonal complement" here means
\texttt{BilinForm.orthogonal}, not "complementary subspace"; do not silently use
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ + dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$} in characteristic $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_arcCycle_subset_support_of_isCirculation]
\lean{CycleSpace.exists_arcCycle_subset_support_of_isCirculation}
\label{CycleSpace.exists_arcCycle_subset_support_of_isCirculation}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle, CycleSpace.cycleSpace}
*If $f$ is a nonzero circulation, then $\| f\|$ contains a
cycle.*

Current cannot enter a dead end: anything that flows must flow round in
a loop.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently trivial for the wrong reason.}  Since \texttt{ArcCycle} has no closure
condition, the goal is satisfied by the one-element list $[a]$ for any $a \in \| f\|$ ---
so this is provable in two lines and means nothing.  Repair \texttt{ArcCycle} before
filling; the skeleton above is for the repaired statement.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_isBond_subset_support_of_mem_bondSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.exists_isBond_subset_support_of_mem_bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.exists_isBond_subset_support_of_mem_bondSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBond, CycleSpace.bondSpace}
*If $g$ is a nonzero potential difference, then $\| g\|$
contains a bond.*

The exact dual of lemma 12.2.1; the two together drive theorem 12.2.

Step 4 is where \texttt{IsBond}'s minimality is consumed --- see that
definition's note about what "minimal among edge cuts" quantifies over.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff]
\lean{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\label{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsArcAcyclic, CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix, CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.restrictCols}
*Let $B$ be a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$.  Then for any $S \subseteq A$,
the columns of $B | S$ are linearly independent if and only if $S$ is acyclic.*

The theorem converting a combinatorial question into a linear-algebraic
one --- and it holds over \textbf{any} field, which is why exercise 12.1.5 is subsumed by
stating \S{}12.1 over \texttt{[Field F]}.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently false.}  With \texttt{ArcCycle} degenerate, \texttt{IsArcAcyclic S $\leftrightarrow$ S = $\emptyset$}, so the
right-hand side says $S = \emptyset$ while the left is true for any independent column set.
Repair \texttt{ArcCycle} first.  Step 4 additionally needs \texttt{cycleCirculation}, also
\texttt{sorry}-bodied.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[basisMatrix_cycleSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff]
\lean{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_cycleSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\label{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_cycleSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix, CycleSpace.IsBond, CycleSpace.cycleSpace, CycleSpace.restrictCols}
*Let $C$ be a basis matrix of $\mathcal{C}$.  Then for any
$S \subseteq A$, the columns of $C | S$ are linearly independent if and only if $S$
contains no bond.*

B&M dispatch this with \emph{"a similar argument"}, but it is genuinely a
second theorem rather than a formal symmetry: $\mathcal{C}$ is defined as a \textbf{kernel} and $\mathcal{B}$
as a \textbf{range}, so step 2 has no counterpart in part (i).

Step 2 is the whole reason this deserves separate treatment;
budget for it rather than expecting the (i) proof to transport.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[finrank_bondSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.finrank_bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.finrank_bondSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph, CycleSpace.bondSpace}
, formula (12.3).  \emph{\texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = $\nu$ - $\omega$}.}

The bond space records the vertex potentials --- $\nu$ of them --- modulo an
additive constant on each of the $\omega$ components, leaving $\nu - \omega$ degrees of freedom.

\textbf{!} Stated over $\mathbb{R}$ specifically, unlike the rest of \S{}12.1 which is
over a general \texttt{[Field F]}; the dimension count is in fact field-independent, so this
could be generalised.  Step 3 is the out-of-chapter import to budget for.  Note the
$\mathbb{N}$-subtraction \texttt{card V - card ConnectedComponent} never truncates, since $\omega \le \nu$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[finrank_cycleSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.finrank_cycleSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.finrank_cycleSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph, CycleSpace.cycleSpace}
, formula (12.4).  \emph{\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$}.}

$\varepsilon - \nu + \omega$ is the \textbf{cycle rank} or first Betti number --- the number of
independent cycles, and exactly the number of arcs outside a maximal forest.  That
count is realised concretely by the fundamental cycles, one per non-tree arc.

\textbf{!} B&M derive this from orthogonality (\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - dim $\mathcal{B}$}),
which is valid over $\mathbb{R}$ but \textbf{not} in characteristic $p$, where the form is
degenerate and the two spaces can overlap (exercise 12.2.4(b)).  The rank--nullity
route of step 1 is field-independent and therefore both simpler and more robust ---
prefer it.
\end{theorem}

The \textbf{fundamental cycle basis} --- the concrete realisation of the claim
that every circulation is a combination of cycle circulations, which is what gave the
cycle space its name.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous.}  Three of the four ingredients --- \texttt{IsMaximalForest},
\texttt{fundamentalCycle}, \texttt{cycleCirculation} --- have \texttt{sorry} bodies.
\end{theorem}

The \textbf{fundamental bond basis}, realising the claim that every

\begin{theorem}[isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree, CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, Matrix.IsUnimodular}
(proof due to Tutte, 1965b).  *The basis matrix $B$ is
unimodular.*

Exactly what theorem 12.4 needs: every full submatrix contributes $0$
or a determinant of absolute value $1$, so squaring and summing counts the spanning
trees.  The proof is due to Tutte (1965b).

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{IsSpanningTree} and \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} both have
\texttt{sorry} bodies.  Note step 4 is where the \emph{axiomatic} reading of
\texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} (\emph{"basis matrix with $B | T$ the identity"}) would pay off
directly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tau_eq_det_mul_transpose]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_mul_transpose}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_mul_transpose}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree, CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, CycleSpace.tau}
\emph{\texttt{$\tau$(G) = det BB'}} (12.6).

The chapter's central computation: the number of spanning trees, a
purely combinatorial quantity, is a determinant.  Compare theorem 2.8's
deletion--contraction recursion, which B&M called impractical for large graphs, and
theorem 2.9's Cayley formula, valid only for complete graphs --- this is general and
efficiently computable.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{tau} (via \texttt{IsSpanningTree}) and \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} both
rest on \texttt{sorry} bodies.  Step 1 is an additional, substantial import.
\end{theorem}

The chapter is organised around such dual pairs --- cycles and bonds,
kernels and ranges, trees and cotrees.

which is stated in this file only for $\mathcal{B}$ (\texttt{basisMatrix\_eq\_restrict\_mul}).  The
cycle version must be proved separately, and --- as noted under theorem 12.2(ii) --- the
$\mathcal{C}$-side arguments are not formal transports of the $\mathcal{B}$-side ones.

\begin{theorem}[tau_eq_det_mul_transpose_cycleSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_mul_transpose_cycleSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_mul_transpose_cycleSpace}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree', CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, CycleSpace.tau}
The spanning trees can be counted from either space --- through the bonds
or through the cycles.  Corollary 12.4 combines the two computations into one
determinant.

\begin{theorem}[tau_eq_det_fromBlocks]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_fromBlocks}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_fromBlocks}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree, CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree', CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, CycleSpace.tau}
\emph{\texttt{$\tau$(G) = $\pm$ det [B; C]}}, the determinant of the square
matrix obtained by stacking a tree-basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$ on top of one of $\mathcal{C}$.

The stacked matrix is square because
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ + dim $\mathcal{C}$ = ($\nu$ - $\omega$) + ($\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$) = $\varepsilon$} --- the two spaces are complementary,
which is theorem 12.1's orthogonality counted dimensionally.

The $\lor$ in the conclusion is the book's $\pm$.  The row index is
${a // a \in T} \oplus {a // a \notin T}$, reindexed to $A$ by \texttt{Equiv.sumCompl} --- that equiv is
canonical here, unlike in exercise 12.2.1(b) where one must be supplied.
\textbf{!} Currently vacuous, resting on \texttt{tau} and both \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} predicates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[matrix_tree_theorem]
\lean{CycleSpace.matrix_tree_theorem}
\label{CycleSpace.matrix_tree_theorem}
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix, CycleSpace.tau}
(implicit in Kirchhoff, 1847).  *\texttt{$\tau$(G) = det KK'},
where $K$ is obtained from the incidence matrix $M$ by deleting any one row.*

The rows of $M$ sum to zero --- every arc contributes $+1$ at its tail
and $-1$ at its head --- so exactly one row is redundant, and discarding it leaves an
independent spanning set of $\mathcal{B}$.  By exercise 12.2.2(a) the product \texttt{MM'} is the

(B&M's \emph{conductance matrix}), so this says every cofactor of the
Laplacian equals $\tau(G)$ --- the form in which the matrix-tree theorem is usually
quoted, and the closed formula for $\tau(G)$ promised back in \S{}2.4.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{tau} and \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph} both rest on \texttt{sorry} bodies.
Step 3 is a genuine restructuring worth doing before any of \S{}12.2 is filled.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isUnimodular_deleteRow]
\lean{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_deleteRow}
\label{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_deleteRow}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix, Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\emph{.  }A matrix $K$ obtained from $M$ by deleting any one row
is unimodular.*

The incidence-matrix counterpart of theorem 12.3, and what upgrades
exercise 12.1.3 into the matrix-tree theorem \texttt{$\tau$(G) = det KK'}.  Note it is proved
\emph{directly}, not via theorem 12.3 --- $K$ is not a tree-basis matrix.

\textbf{!} Step 3's leaf induction is the real work and has no counterpart
in theorem 12.3's slick change-of-basis argument.  \textbf{!} The statement lacks a
connectivity hypothesis, unlike \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_deleteRow}; step 2 uses that $K$ is a
basis matrix, which \emph{does} need \texttt{hconn} --- so either add it or find a route through
step 3 alone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose]
\lean{CycleSpace.lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose}
\label{CycleSpace.lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
*The conductance matrix $C$ of a loopless graph $G$
satisfies \texttt{C = MM'}, where $M$ is the incidence matrix of any orientation of $G$.*

\textbf{*} \textbf{The cheapest win in the file} --- a direct computation, no dependency
on the defective definitions.  This is what Mathlib calls the \textbf{Laplacian}; B&M call
it the \emph{conductance matrix}.  Notably the \emph{orientation drops out} --- the signs cancel
--- so it is an invariant of the undirected graph, as it must be.

Step 3's parallel-arc caveat is the one thing to pin down before
starting; everything else is \texttt{Finset.sum} manipulation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tau_eq_det_lapMatrix_deleteRowCol]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_lapMatrix_deleteRowCol}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_lapMatrix_deleteRowCol}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.tau}
*All cofactors of the conductance matrix $C$ are equal
to $\tau(G)$.*

The form in which the matrix-tree theorem is normally stated: *the
number of spanning trees is any cofactor of the Laplacian*.  It finally delivers, in
full generality, the closed formula for $\tau(G)$ that \S{}2.4 promised and that theorem
2.9 gave only for complete graphs.

This states the \emph{principal} $(y,y)$-minor, which is what the
matrix-tree theorem gives directly and what every application uses.  B&M claim
\textbf{all} cofactors equal $\tau(G)$, including the non-principal ones; that full statement
is \texttt{tau\_eq\_lapMatrix\_cofactor} directly below, and this principal case is the one to
prove first.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.tau}
, full form.  *All cofactors of the conductance matrix $C$
are equal to $\tau(G)$.*

\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_lapMatrix\_deleteRowCol} above states only the
principal $(y,y)$-minor.  The triage (\texttt{log/graphtheory-EXERCISE\_TRIAGE.md} \S{}A.11)
recorded this as a fidelity gap and recommended stating the exercise as written.  The
general form is the one usually cited, because it is what licenses deleting \emph{any} row
and \emph{any} column --- the principal case alone does not.

\textbf{!} Deleting row $i$ and column $j$ for $i \ne j$ leaves a matrix whose
row and column index types are the \emph{different} subtypes ${v // v \ne i}$ and
${v // v \ne j}$, so \texttt{Matrix.det} does not apply to it.  A reindexing equiv $e$ between
the two is therefore threaded through explicitly --- the same device
\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks\_K} uses further down this file for the same reason.  Because $e$
is not canonical it fixes the column order only up to a permutation, so the conclusion
is stated up to sign, absorbing $(-1)^(i+j)$ and \texttt{sign e} together.  Taking $i = j$ and
\texttt{e = Equiv.refl} recovers the principal case above.

\textbf{!} Currently vacuous via \texttt{tau} and \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}, exactly as the principal case
is.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[incMatrix_isTotallyUnimodular_iff_isBipartite]
\lean{CycleSpace.incMatrix_isTotallyUnimodular_iff_isBipartite}
\label{CycleSpace.incMatrix_isTotallyUnimodular_iff_isBipartite}
\leanok
*The incidence matrix of a simple graph $G$ is totally
unimodular if and only if $G$ is bipartite.*

\textbf{!} Note this is the \emph{unoriented} $0/1$ incidence matrix of \S{}1.3, \textbf{not}
the signed one of this chapter --- the signed version is always totally unimodular, for
every graph.  The classical characterisation underlying the integrality of bipartite
matching linear programs, and it links back to theorem 1.2: bipartite means no odd
cycle.

\textbf{*} Independent of every defective definition in this file --- it
mentions only \texttt{SimpleGraph.incMatrix} and \texttt{IsBipartite}, both Mathlib.  Together with
exercise 12.2.2(a), one of the two items that can be filled today.  Step 2's
determinant computation is the concrete part.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau]
\lean{CycleSpace.finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau}
\label{CycleSpace.finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.cycleSpace, CycleSpace.tau}
(H. Shank).  *Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$.
Then \texttt{dim($\mathcal{B}$\_F $\cap$ $\mathcal{C}$\_F) > 0} if and only if $p \mid \tau(G)$.*

Over $\mathbb{R}$ the two spaces are orthogonal complements and meet only in
zero.  In characteristic $p$ the dot form is \textbf{degenerate} --- a vector can be
orthogonal to itself --- so they may genuinely overlap, and Shank's result says the
overlap is nontrivial exactly when $p \mid \tau(G)$.  A purely arithmetic property of
$\tau(G)$ detected by a linear-algebraic degeneracy --- a striking illustration of the
chapter's theme.

\textbf{!} Step 1 must \textbf{not} be derived from orthogonality (\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ =
$\varepsilon$ - dim $\mathcal{B}$}), which is exactly what fails here; use the rank--nullity argument
recorded under \texttt{finrank\_cycleSpace}.  Getting this wrong would make the proof
circular --- the whole point is that the two spaces are \emph{not} complementary.
\end{theorem}
